name: Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota)
place: 1st-degree chiefdom of Biatsota II, Mvele canton (Mbam-et-Kim, Centre)
overview: The Biatsota, Mvele of Ntui, live in good neighbourliness with the Djané, Nkulutu and Biindandjengué, and speak Ossananga, whose speakers are found as far as the edges of Adamawa. Catholics for a long time, they live from cocoa, fishing, trade and food crops, and share many customs with the Eton.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Group integrated with its neighbours (Djané, Nkulutu, Biindandjengué), who speak closely related speech varieties, differing mainly in pronunciation.
Ossananga is found as far as the boundary between Ntui and Ngaoundéré.
Marriages within and outside the grouping; since kinship is very extensive in the village, many marry outside.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land; Catholicism has long dominated.
Small group, hence questions of land ownership.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: A chief and notables, including the patriarchs, lead the grouping; the chief decides with the agreement of his court.
Anyone, even if unmarried, can make suggestions at assemblies.
Clan A does not inherit from clan B: each grouping has its chief, and succession is hereditary.
One uncovers one's head to greet the chief; the wife owes obedience to her husband.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Extended kinship, mostly patrilineal; the wife joins her husband.
Boys and girls become adults at the age of majority, 18 according to tradition.
Steps: getting to know the future spouses, introduction to the in-laws (“knocking at the door”), bride price, which makes the wife's entry into her in-law family official.
Palm wine opens the marriage discussions; the kola nut seals the friendship between families.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: No more ancestor worship or sacred places: modernity has replaced them.
Birth is a joy that enlarges the group; death, a loss willed by God.
Taboos: viper and certain meats; pregnant women and children do not eat rat; only the elders eat rat and viper.
Theft is punished according to the law.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: cocoa, fishing, trade. Women: food crops (sweet potato, cocoyam, yams).
The land belongs to the community and the chief is its custodian.
No craft tradition.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: The obom, an outfit of bark and banana leaves, has disappeared with modernity.
Traditional medicine is used less and less.
Beauty: diligence for men, conduct for women; seduction through dance and good conduct.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: The tam-tam is beaten at funerals and the balafon is played at weddings; modern rhythms have taken over.
End-of-year festival to celebrate and implore the grace of the Lord.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The Biatsota share their customs with their Eton neighbours and speak Ossananga and Eton fluently.

sections.title: The names
items: Twins' names: Dimi and Njo'o, Bella and Njoa.
A name may be changed in case of disagreement with the father or if the child does not resemble his or her name.
The parent takes the name of his child: Ndongo, father of Biloa, becomes “Biloa Ndongo”.
The ancestor is Tsota, of the mvele grouping.

ethnonymes.meaning: Related to the Manguissa among the Eton

lessons.title: Who are the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Group integrated with its neighbours (Djané, Nkulutu, Biindandjengué), who speak closely related speech varieties, differing mainly in pronunciation. • Ossananga is found as far as the boundary between Ntui and Ngaoundéré. • Marriages within and outside the groupement; since kinship is very extensive in the village, many marry outside. • Ancestral land; Catholicism has long been dominant. • Small group, hence questions of land ownership.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Biatsota, Mvele of Ntui, live in good neighbourliness with the Djané, Nkulutu and Biindandjengué, and speak Ossananga, whose speakers are found as far as the edges of Adamawa. Catholics for a long time, they live from cocoa, fishing, trade and food crops, and share many customs with the Eton.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)

steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.instruction: A chief and notables, including the patriarchs, govern the grouping; the chief decides with the agreement of his court. lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: pistachio dishes, groundnut dishes. • Drinks: arki (cassava and maize), palm wine. • Men: cocoa, fishing, trade. Women: food crops (sweet potato, cocoyam, yams).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) mainly eat pistachio-seed dishes, groundnut dishes. Traditional drinks: arki, palm wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

activities.instruction: Choose the most representative dance: participants, instruments, attire, gestures.

activities.title: I understand
activities.instruction: Explain whether it is a dance of joy, mourning, initiation or war.

activities.title: I practise
activities.instruction: With your group, act out the dance in front of the class.

student.memo: Among the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota), traditional dances (mourning dances with the tam-tam, wedding dances with the balafon) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: tam-tam, balafon. Festival(s): end-of-year celebration.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Men: cocoa, fishing, trade. Women: food crops (sweet potato, cocoyam, yams). • Land belongs to the community and the chief is its custodian. • No craft tradition.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: cocoa, fishing, trade. Women: food crops (sweet potato, cocoyam, yams). Land belongs to the community and the chief is its custodian.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.title: I calculate

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

student.memo: Men: cocoa, fishing, trade. Women: food crops (sweet potato, cocoyam, yams). Land belongs to the community and the chief is its custodian.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: rat pour les femmes enceintes et les enfants

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • No more ancestor cult or sacred places: modernity has replaced them. • Birth is a joy that enlarges the group; death, a loss willed by God. • Prohibitions: viper and certain meats; pregnant women and children do not eat rat; only elders eat rat and viper. • Theft is punished according to the law.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No more ancestral cult or sacred places: modernity has replaced them. Birth is a joy that enlarges the group; death, a loss willed by God.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: No more ancestral cult or sacred places: modernity has replaced them. Birth is a joy that enlarges the group; death, a loss willed by God.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Ossananga
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The language of the community is Ossananga. • Greeting formulas: Wahou ma’a = Hello (neutral formula, at any time); Woubè tèh = morning greeting (one person); Ngoubè tèh = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Emossi, Moba, Motat, Moené, Motano. • The ancestor is Tsota, of the mvele groupement. • The Biatsota share their customs with their Eton neighbours and speak both Ossananga and Eton fluently.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Ossananga are the first steps towards communicating with the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Ossananga.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Ossananga are the first steps towards communicating with the Mvele de Ntui (Biatsota). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
